docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Annotated data structure for complex networks annnet

annnet (Annotated Network) is a high-expressivity data structure for networks. One container holds simple graphs, multilayer networks and hypergraphs, together with their annotations. It is designed for systems biology, network biology, omics integration, computational social science, and any domain that needs fully flexible graph semantics, with stable storage and interoperability.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install "annnet[polars,networkx,storage]"

This installs annnet with the Polars tables, the NetworkX backend and the native file format. The core package alone is pip install annnet. For all optional extras, see Installation.

docs.title: 2. Try it
docs.text:
Build a small signaling network from a table, select the confident interactions, run a NetworkX algorithm on the same object, and save the result:

import annnet as an
import polars as pl

interactions = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        'source': ['EGFR', 'GRB2', 'SOS1', 'KRAS', 'BRAF', 'PTEN'],
        'target': ['GRB2', 'SOS1', 'KRAS', 'BRAF', 'MAPK1', 'AKT1'],
        'sign': [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, -1],
        'confidence': [0.95, 0.9, 0.8, 0.9, 0.7, 0.85],
    }
)

anet = an.from_edge_frame(interactions, sign='sign', directed=True)
print(anet.summary())  # 8 nodes, 6 edges

confident = anet.view(edges=anet.E.select(confidence__gte=0.85))
print(len(confident.N), len(confident.E))  # 7 nodes, 4 edges

scores = anet.nx.betweenness_centrality(anet)
anet.attrs.update('nodes', {n: {'betweenness': v} for n, v in scores.items()})

anet.write('signaling.annnet')
anet2 = an.read('signaling.annnet')

The Quickstart goes through the same steps with a larger table, and explains views, annotations and the saved file.

docs.title: 3. Learn more
docs.text:
• Guide, five notebooks with concepts, mathematics and runnable code: graph model and matrices · annotations and views · slices · layers · computation and storage
  • Tutorials, complete analyses: multi-condition causal signaling · TGF-beta fibrosis response, and integrations with OmniPath, Cytoscape, PyG and CORNETO
  • API reference: exact signatures and options
  • Community: how to contribute to the docs and the code

docs.title: Main features
docs.text:
annnet unifies rich graph semantics, annotated tables and lossless storage. Download the figure as PDF.

At the core is a sparse incidence-based representation that supports mixed graph types within the same object. Edges are first-class entities with stable identifiers, and graph type (directed, undirected, hyperedge) is a property of each edge rather than the container. Around this core, annnet organizes metadata as typed tables and exposes higher-level constructs such as slices and multilayer structure without duplicating the underlying graph.

  • One object for heterogeneous graphs

    Represent simple graphs, digraphs, signed edges, hyperedges, self-loops, parallel edges, and edge-entity relations without switching data models.

    See: hyperedges in the guide · edge as an endpoint · adding edges

  • Typed annotation tables

    Store node, edge, slice, layer, and edge-slice metadata in indexed tabular structures instead of flat per-object dictionaries.

    See: annotations in the guide · OmniPath table example · attributes

  • Named slices for conditions and views

    Define condition-specific or context-specific graph views without copying the full topology, with optional per-slice edge-weight overrides.

    See: slices in the guide · multi-condition example · slices

  • Multilayer network support

    Work with aspects, layer tuples, node-layer membership, intra-layer edges, inter-layer edges, and coupling structure as part of the core model.

    See: layers in the guide · supra-adjacency · layers

  • All popular graph libraries, without conversion work

    Run NetworkX, igraph and graph-tool algorithms directly on an annnet graph through anet.nx, anet.ig and anet.gt. annnet converts lazily and stays the canonical representation.

    See: backends in the guide · PyG example · backend accessors

  • Native, loss-aware storage

    Persist topology, annotations, and metadata together in a format designed for round-trip fidelity and scalable IO.

    See: storage in the guide · Cytoscape example · format comparison

docs.title: Why annnet
docs.text:
Many real-world networks are structurally heterogeneous and context-dependent. A single dataset may combine directed and undirected interactions, signed edges, higher-order relations, and multiple contextual or temporal conditions. Standard graph libraries handle topology and algorithms well, but typically treat attributes as flat, per-object dictionaries without schema, indexing, or efficient bulk operations. This makes it difficult to manage annotations, compare conditions, or preserve structure across analysis steps.

annnet keeps graph topology, annotation tables, and graph views aligned in a single container. It does not replace the existing graph libraries: it makes the most popular ones (NetworkX, igraph, graph-tool) available on the same object, and exchanges data with formats and tools such as Cytoscape, GraphML, SBML and PyTorch Geometric. You keep one consistent data model and still use the established tooling.

The design follows the matrix-plus-annotation pattern of omics containers such as AnnData, and adapts it to graphs with heterogeneous topology. annnet is most useful where graph structure is only one part of the data model, and where annotations, conditions, or multiple representations must be handled explicitly:

  • Systems biology and omics integration

    Model regulatory, signaling, metabolic, and cross-modal networks with typed metadata and multiple analysis contexts.

    See: TGF-beta fibrosis example

  • Condition-specific and temporal networks

    Keep one shared graph with named slices for perturbations, time points, cohorts, or filtered analytical views.

    See: slices in the guide · multi-condition example

  • Multimodal and layered data

    Represent networks across modalities, resolutions, or time as explicit multilayer objects rather than ad hoc conventions.

    See: several aspects and windows

  • Exchange with existing tooling

    Move between annnet and standard graph ecosystems, file formats, and ML pipelines without flattening the original structure too early.

    See: Cytoscape · PyG · CORNETO

annnet is part of sysbioverse, an ecosystem of free open source packages for molecular systems biology. The packages share data structures, design principles and workflows, and build on the scverse ecosystem for single-cell omics analysis.

docs.title: Installation guide
docs.text: annnet is designed to stay lightweight by default. The base package only requires NumPy, SciPy, Narwhals, and pkg-infra, and everything heavier is exposed as an optional extra.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+
  • pip for standard installs
  • uv if you want a fast local or development workflow
  • git if you want to install from GitHub

Check your environment:

python --version
pip --version
uv --version
git --version

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
If you just want the core package:

pip install annnet

This gives you the core graph data structure and algorithms without pulling in backend, plotting, storage, or ML dependencies you may never use.

docs.title: Choose your extras
docs.text: Install only the extras you need. annnet exposes both single-purpose extras and broader install bundles.

docs.title: Tabular data backends
docs.text:
Single extras:

pip install "annnet[polars]"
pip install "annnet[pandas]"
pip install "annnet[pyarrow]"
  • polars: Polars, the recommended dataframe backend for annnet tables and annotations
  • pandas: pandas dataframe support
  • pyarrow: Apache Arrow table support and parquet-related tabular workflows

If more than one dataframe backend is installed, annnet has a built-in preference order. You can still choose a backend globally or for graph construction when needed; see the support helper reference.

docs.title: Graph backends
docs.text:
Single extras:

pip install "annnet[networkx]"
pip install "annnet[igraph]"
pip install "annnet[pyg]"

Bundle:

pip install "annnet[backends]"
  • networkx: interoperability with NetworkX and access to its algorithms
  • igraph: interoperability with python-igraph
  • pyg: PyTorch Geometric support
  • backends: installs the pip-installable graph backends networkx and igraph

annnet also supports graph-tool. graph-tool is not available on PyPI: install it separately with Pixi, conda, or your system package manager.

docs.title: Plotting backends
docs.text:
Single extras:

pip install "annnet[matplotlib]"
pip install "annnet[pydot]"
pip install "annnet[graphviz]"

Bundle:

pip install "annnet[plot]"
  • matplotlib: plots with Matplotlib
  • pydot: DOT export and plots with pydot
  • graphviz: Python bindings for Graphviz
  • plot: installs all pip-installable plotting backends together

When plot(..., backend="auto") is used, annnet selects the first installed backend in its plotting preference order. You can still choose a plotting backend globally or for individual plotting calls; see the support helper reference.

docs.title: I/O extras
docs.text:
Single extras:

pip install "annnet[excel]"
pip install "annnet[parquet]"
pip install "annnet[zarr_io]"
pip install "annnet[sbml]"

Bundles:

pip install "annnet[io]"
pip install "annnet[storage]"
pip install "annnet[metabo]"
  • excel: Excel import/export support
  • parquet: Parquet I/O support with pyarrow
  • zarr_io: .annnet storage support with Zarr and numcodecs
  • sbml: SBML parsing support
  • io: broader I/O bundle including pandas, openpyxl, pyarrow, zarr, numcodecs, lxml, and toml
  • storage: storage-oriented subset for parquet/zarr/pandas workflows
  • metabo: metabolomics bundle with SBML, COBRApy, and Graphviz

docs.title: Other install bundles
docs.text:
pip install "annnet[all]"
  • all: broad pip-installable runtime bundle, excluding non-PyPI dependencies and PyG Use all if you want a batteries-included pip install and do not mind a larger environment.

docs.title: Install from GitHub with uv
docs.text:
Use this if you want the latest repository version before the next PyPI release:

uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install "git+https://github.com/saezlab/annnet.git"

If you want extras as well, use the package URL in the same way you would use an extra on PyPI, for example:

uv pip install "annnet[all] @ git+https://github.com/saezlab/annnet.git"

docs.title: Local editable install with uv
docs.text:
For development or documentation work with pip-installable dependencies only, clone the repository and install it in editable mode:

git clone https://github.com/saezlab/annnet.git
cd annnet
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e .

For a fuller local environment:

uv sync --group dev --group tests --group docs

You can also add runtime extras you care about:

uv sync --group dev --group tests
uv pip install -e ".[networkx,igraph,polars,sbml,parquet]"

docs.title: Run tests with uv
docs.text:
From the repository root:

uv sync --group tests
uv run pytest -vv

docs.title: Use Pixi for non-pip dependencies
docs.text:
Use Pixi when you want the repository's fuller development environment, especially for dependencies that are not reliably available from PyPI such as graph-tool.

pixi install -e gt
pixi run -e gt test-gt

The Pixi environment:

  • installs annnet editable with the repository test dependency group
  • provides graph-tool from conda-forge
  • is the right path for running tests that depend on non-pip packages

If you want the full test suite inside the Pixi environment, run:

pixi run -e gt test-all

docs.title: Build and serve the docs
docs.text:
From a repository checkout:

uv sync --group docs
uv run --group docs python -m mkdocs serve --dev-addr 127.0.0.1:8000

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. This executes the Quickstart and the five Guide notebooks; Tutorials render their saved outputs. For a strict build without the preview server:

uv run --group docs python -m mkdocs build --strict

The site is written to site/. See Contributing to the documentation for faster previews, notebook editing, and the public-site configuration.

docs.title: Quickstart¶
docs.text:
Start with an interaction table, look at what annnet imported, select a subset, and save the annotated graph. The example uses a small synthetic teaching dataset: 11 interactions among 10 nodes, with two separately identified EGFR–GRB2 records.

Install annnet with Polars tables, the native file format and Graphviz plots:

pip install "annnet[polars,storage,graphviz]"

The Graphviz plots also need the dot program of Graphviz on your system.

docs.title: Load the table¶
docs.text: Read the interaction table. The columns are edge_id, source, target, effect, confidence, and evidence.

docs.title: Import the network¶
docs.text: Map the identifier and effect columns explicitly, and put all interactions in a slice named prior:

docs.title: Inspect and select¶
docs.text: The edge table shows the endpoints of each edge next to its annotations:

docs.title: Add an annotation¶
docs.text: Write through anet.attrs to change the graph:

docs.title: Save and reopen¶
docs.text: The native format keeps identities, annotations, and slice membership. The example writes into a temporary directory; use your own path to keep the file. The writer does not replace an existing file unless you give overwrite=True.

docs.title: Next steps¶
docs.text: Continue with Annotations, selections, and views for filters and materialization, or with Slices to attach results for several conditions. The Guide also covers the graph model, layers, and computation and storage.

docs.title: Join us
docs.text:
There are many useful ways to contribute to annnet besides writing package code. Improvements to the documentation, examples, and contributor workflows all help move the project forward.

  • Contribute to the documentation

    Improve guides, explanations, examples, and API docs when something is missing, confusing, or out of date.

    Open the docs guide

  • Contribute to the package code

    Work on bug fixes, tests, new features, and package internals when you are ready to contribute to the library itself.

    Open the code guide

docs.title: How we work
docs.text:
For larger changes, start with a short discussion before implementation so we can confirm scope and avoid duplicate work.

Common contribution paths:

  • Bug reports
  • New feature requests
  • Documentation improvements
  • Package and test-suite changes

docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text: Thank you for considering to contribute to the project! This guide will help you to get started with the development of the project. If you have any questions, please feel free to ask them in the issue tracker on GitHub.

docs.title: Small Contributions
docs.text: If you want to contribute a small change (e.g., a bugfix), you can probably immediately go ahead and create a pull request. For more substantial changes or additions, please read on.

docs.title: Larger Contributions
docs.text: If you want to contribute a larger change, please start from the Join us page and open a discussion first. This will allow us to discuss the change and make sure that it fits into the project. It can happen that development for a feature is already in progress, so it is important to check first to avoid duplicate work. If you have any questions, feel free to approach us in any way you like.

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text:
annnet uses standard pyproject.toml project metadata with Hatchling as the build backend. Development, documentation, and test dependencies are declared as dependency groups in pyproject.toml and are installed with uv.

For a local development environment:

git clone https://github.com/saezlab/annnet.git
cd annnet
uv sync --group dev --group tests --group docs

Run commands through uv run so they use the synchronized environment:

uv run pytest
uv run ruff check annnet tests
uv run python -m mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Dependency groups and extras
docs.text:
Runtime dependencies and optional extras live under [project] and [project.optional-dependencies] in pyproject.toml. Development-only groups live under [dependency-groups].

Use the existing groups when possible:

  • dev: contributor tooling such as Ruff, pre-commit, mypy, and twine.
  • tests: pytest, coverage, and test-only optional runtime dependencies.
  • docs: MkDocs and documentation build dependencies.

If a new dependency is required at runtime, add it to the appropriate [project.optional-dependencies] extra or to the base [project] dependencies only when it is needed by the core package. If a dependency is only needed for tests, docs, or local tooling, add it to the corresponding dependency group.

docs.title: graph-tool and Pixi
docs.text:
graph-tool is not available from PyPI. The repository defines a Pixi gt environment for graph-tool tests:

pixi install -e gt
pixi run -e gt test-gt

To run the full test suite inside the Pixi environment:

pixi run -e gt test-all

docs.title: Code quality and formal requirements
docs.text:
For ensuring code quality, the following tools are used:

  • Ruff for linting, import sorting, and formatting rules.
  • pre-commit for running repository hooks locally.
  • mypy for type checking where enabled.
  • tox for CI-like local test, lint, readme, and docs environments.

We recommend configuring your IDE to execute Ruff on save/type, which will automatically keep your code clean and fix some linting errors as you type. This is made possible by the fast execution of Ruff and removes the need to run a dedicated pre-commit step. For instance, in VSCode or Cursor, you can add this to your .vscode/settings.json:

{
    "editor.formatOnType": true,
    "editor.formatOnSave": true,
    "editor.codeActionsOnSave": {
        "source.fixAll.ruff": "explicit",
        "source.organizeImports.ruff": "explicit"
    },
    "editor.defaultFormatter": "charliermarsh.ruff"
}

Alternatively, pre-commit hooks can be used to automatically or manually run these tools before each commit. They are defined in .pre-commit-config.yaml. To install the hooks run uv run pre-commit install. The hooks are then executed before each commit. For running the hook for all project files (not only the changed ones) run uv run pre-commit run --all-files. Our CI runs the pre-commit hooks, so running them locally is a good way to check if your code conforms to the formatting rules.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The project uses pytest for testing. To run the tests, use the test dependency group:

uv sync --group tests
uv run pytest

Run graph-tool tests through Pixi:

pixi run -e gt test-gt

Please add or update tests for behavior changes before submitting a pull request.

The existing tests can also help you to understand how the code works. If you have any questions, please feel free to ask them in the issue tracker or on Zulip.

Before submitting a pull request, please make sure that all tests pass and that the documentation builds correctly.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
We use semantic versioning for the project. This means that the version number is incremented according to the following scheme:

  • Increment the major version number if you make incompatible API changes.

  • Increment the minor version number if you add functionality in a backwards- compatible manner. Since we are still in the 0.x.y version range, most of the significant changes will increase the minor version number.

  • Increment the patch version number if you make backwards-compatible bug fixes.

Version updates are handled by the maintainers. Please do not increment versions in pull requests by default.

docs.title: Finding an issue to contribute to
docs.text:
If you are brand new to annnet or open-source development, we recommend searching the GitHub "Issues" tab to find issues that interest you. Unassigned issues labeled Docs and good first are typically good for newer contributors.

Once you've found an interesting issue, it's a good idea to assign the issue to yourself, so nobody else duplicates the work on it.

If for whatever reason you are not able to continue working with the issue, please unassign it, so other people know it's available again. If you want to work on an issue that is currently assigned but you're unsure whether work is actually being done, feel free to kindly ask the current assignee if you can take over (please allow at least a week of inactivity before getting in touch).

docs.title: Tips for a successful pull request
docs.text:
To improve the chances of your pull request being reviewed, you should:

  • Reference an open issue for non-trivial changes to clarify the PR's purpose.
  • Ensure you have appropriate tests. Tests should be the focus of any PR (apart from documentation changes).
  • Keep your pull requests as simple as possible. Larger PRs take longer to review.
  • Ensure that CI is in a green state. Reviewers may tell you to fix the CI before looking at anything else.

docs.title: Version control, Git, and GitHub
docs.text:
annnet is hosted on GitHub, and to contribute, you will need to sign up for a free GitHub account. We use Git for version control to allow many people to work together on the project.

If you are new to Git, you can reference some of these resources for learning Git. Feel free to reach out to the contributor community for help if needed:

  • Git documentation.

The project follows a forking workflow further described on this page whereby contributors fork the repository, make changes and then create a Pull Request. So please be sure to read and follow all the instructions in this guide.

If you are new to contributing to projects through forking on GitHub, take a look at the GitHub documentation for contributing to projects. GitHub provides a quick tutorial using a test repository that may help you become more familiar with forking a repository, cloning a fork, creating a feature branch, pushing changes and making Pull Requests.

Below are some useful resources for learning more about forking and Pull Requests on GitHub:

  • the GitHub documentation for forking a repo.

  • the GitHub documentation for collaborating with Pull Requests.

  • the GitHub documentation for working with forks.

There are also many unwritten rules and conventions that are helpful in interacting with other open-source contributors. These lessons from PyOpenSci are a good resource for learning more about how to interact with other open-source contributors in scientific computing.

docs.title: Getting started with Git
docs.text: GitHub has instructions for installing git, setting up your SSH key, and configuring git. All these steps need to be completed before you can work seamlessly between your local repository and GitHub.

docs.title: Create a fork of annnet
docs.text:
You will need your own fork of annnet in order to eventually open a Pull Request. Go to the annnet project page and hit the Fork button. Please uncheck the box to copy only the main branch before selecting Create Fork. You will then want to clone your fork to your machine.

git clone https://github.com/your-user-name/annnet.git
cd annnet
git remote add upstream https://github.com/saezlab/annnet.git
git fetch upstream

This creates the directory annnet and connects your repository to the upstream (main project) annnet repository. They have the same name, but your local repository and fork are separate from the upstream repository.

docs.title: Creating a feature branch
docs.text:
Your local main branch should always reflect the current state of annnet repository. First ensure it's up-to-date with the main annnet repository.

git checkout main
git pull upstream main --ff-only

Then, create a feature branch for making your changes. For example, we are going to create a branch called my-new-feature-for-annnet

git checkout -b my-new-feature-for-annnet

This changes your working branch from main to the my-new-feature-for-annnet branch. Keep any changes in this branch specific to one bug or feature so it is clear what the branch brings to annnet. You can have many feature branches and switch between them using the git checkout command.

docs.title: Making code changes
docs.text:
Before modifying any code, ensure you follow the contributing environment guidelines to set up an appropriate development environment.

When making changes, follow these annnet-specific guidelines:

  1. Keep changes of that branch/PR focused on a single feature or bug fix.

  2. Follow roughly the conventional commit message conventions.

docs.title: Pushing your changes
docs.text:
When you want your committed changes to appear publicly on your GitHub page, you can push your forked feature branch's commits to your forked repository on GitHub.

Now your code is on GitHub, but it is not yet a part of the annnet project. For that to happen, a Pull Request (PR) needs to be submitted.

docs.title: Opening a Pull Request (PR)
docs.text:
If everything looks good according to the general guidelines, you are ready to make a Pull Request. A Pull Request is how code from your fork becomes available to the project maintainers to review and merge into the project to appear in the next release. To submit a Pull Request:

  1. Navigate to your repository on GitHub.

  2. Click on the Compare & Pull Request button.

  3. You can then click on Commits and Files Changed to make sure everything looks okay one last time.

  4. Write a descriptive title that includes prefixes. annnet uses a convention for title prefixes, most commonly, feat: for features, fix: for bug fixes, and refactor: for refactoring.

  5. Write a description of your changes in the Preview Discussion tab. This description will inform the reviewers about the changes you made, so please include all relevant information, including the motivation, implementation details, and references to any issues that you are addressing.

  6. Make sure to Allow edits from maintainers; this allows the maintainers to make changes to your PR directly, which is useful if you are not sure how to fix the PR.

  7. Click Send Pull Request.

  8. Optionally, you can assign reviewers to your PR, if you know who should review it.

This request then goes to the repository maintainers, and they will review the code.

docs.title: Updating your Pull Request
docs.text: Based on the review you get on your pull request, you will probably need to make some changes to the code. You can follow the steps above again to address any feedback and update your pull request.

docs.title: Parallel changes in the upstream main branch
docs.text:
In case of simultaneous changes to the upstream code, it is important that these changes are reflected in your pull request. To update your feature branch with changes in the annnet main branch, run:

    git checkout my-new-feature-for-annnet
    git fetch upstream
    git merge upstream/main

If there are no conflicts (or they could be fixed automatically), a file with a default commit message will open, and you can simply save and quit this file.

If there are merge conflicts, you need to resolve those conflicts. See here for an explanation on how to do this.

Once the conflicts are resolved, run:

  1. git add -u to stage any files you've updated;
  2. git commit to finish the merge.

After the feature branch has been updated locally, you can now update your pull request by pushing to the branch on GitHub:

    git push origin my-new-feature-for-annnet

Any git push will automatically update your pull request with your branch's changes and restart the Continuous Integration checks.

docs.title: Contributing to the documentation
docs.text: Edit Markdown pages under docs/ and topic notebooks under docs/guide/. The API reference under docs/reference/ renders the package's NumPy-style docstrings with mkdocstrings.

docs.title: Where content belongs
docs.text:
• Quickstart: one short import, inspect, select, and save workflow.
  • Guide: five topic notebooks. Explain a concept, its mathematics where needed, and its practical API in the same notebook. Extend the relevant topic before adding another tutorial about it.
  • Tutorials: complete analyses and integrations, all in docs/tutorials/. Each one has its environment file in docs/tutorials/environments/.
  • API Reference: signatures, input forms, file-format details, and migration.
  • Community: contribution instructions and implementation reports.

Prefer imported data for workflows. Use a small manually constructed graph when it makes a specific structural rule or calculation easier to verify. State data provenance and distinguish illustrative values from measured results.

docs.title: Preview locally
docs.text:
From the repository root:

uv sync --group docs
uv run --group docs python -m mkdocs serve --dev-addr 127.0.0.1:8000

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. MkDocs rebuilds after edits. The default build executes the five Guide notebooks and fails on execution errors. Case studies and integration examples render their saved outputs using the example environments when run separately.

For faster prose and layout work, render the notebooks' saved outputs:

ANNNET_EXECUTE_NOTEBOOKS=false uv run --group docs python -m mkdocs serve

Re-enable execution before validating changes to notebook code. Refresh stored outputs in Jupyter with Restart Kernel and Run All Cells, then save.

docs.title: Check before submitting
docs.text:
uv run --group docs python -m mkdocs build --strict
uv run --group docs python -m mkdocs build --strict -f mkdocs-online.yml

The second command checks the public navigation, which excludes experimental reference pages. Both write the site to site/. Check rendered formulas, table outputs, downloads, and links as well as the build result. Notebook links should use source-relative paths, such as ../reference/core/layers.md; the build hook rewrites them to website URLs.

Keep one authoritative explanation per topic. When moving a published page, update internal links and its redirect in tools/mkdocs_hooks.py so existing bookmarks still work.

docs.title: Guide
docs.text:
annnet keeps graph structure, annotations, and analysis contexts in one object. These five notebooks explain how those parts work together. Each topic includes the concepts, relevant mathematics, working examples, and links to the API.

Start with the quickstart, then read the topics you need:

Topic What you will learn Graph model and matrices Node and edge identity, hyperedges, incidence coefficients, adjacency, and traversal. Annotations, selections, and views Where attributes live, table access, filtering, live views, and materialized graphs. Slices and analysis contexts Keep a prior network and condition-specific selections and results together. Layers Aspects and placements, importing a multilayer graph, measurements, coupling, supra-matrices, and dynamics. Computation and storage Run backend algorithms, attach results, choose an export, save an analysis, and understand history limits.

Slices select existing identities; layers place identities in explicit coordinates. Use slices when two analyses select or annotate the same interactions. Use layers when an entity's placement in a condition, mechanism, or timepoint is itself part of the graph. The two can be used together.

docs.title: Run the notebooks
docs.text:
Install the package with the dependencies used by the guide:

python -m pip install 'annnet[polars,networkx,storage]' jupyterlab

Alternatively, use the conda environment. Download a notebook from its page, and put the three sample CSV files in a data/ directory beside it. In a repository checkout, the files are already in docs/guide/data. Run the cells in order; each notebook imports its own graph and does not depend on the other notebooks.

The data are small and synthetic, so these notebooks require no external data service. For longer analyses with biological data or other software, see Tutorials.

docs.title: Annotations, selections, and views¶
docs.text:
An imported network has values attached to different objects. This notebook explains where those values belong, how to read and update them, and how a predicate becomes a live graph view. The running question is which supported, inhibitory interactions to keep for analysis.

Requires annnet[polars,storage] and the guide data in a data/ directory beside this notebook. This notebook does not depend on the other guide chapters.

docs.title: Inspect the input¶
docs.text: The CSV contains one evidence record per row. Two rows share the EGFR–GRB2 endpoints but have different IDs and confidence scores. Retaining the IDs lets later results distinguish those records.

docs.title: Put values at the right address¶
docs.text:
The tutorial network has a confidence score for each evidence record. That is an edge attribute. An activity estimated separately in control and treatment belongs to an edge-slice pair. A measured response for ERK in the treatment layer belongs to a node-layer pair.

anet.attrs provides the same reading and writing operations at eight addresses:

Address Key Example nodes Node ID Display label or identifier namespace. edges Edge ID Confidence, source resource, or effect sign. slices Slice ID Method and parameters for an analysis result. edge_slices (slice_id, edge_id) Activity of an edge in one result. aspects Aspect name Description of a condition axis. elementary_layers (aspect, label) Metadata for the label treated. layers Layer coordinate Metadata for a complete coordinate such as ('6h', 'treated'). node_layers (node_id, layer_coordinate) A node's measurement in that layer.

Graph-wide metadata goes in anet.uns, a dictionary suitable for an analysis description, source information, or parameter settings. A generic node attribute applies to the node across its placements; use node_layers when the value differs between them.

docs.title: Import identities and annotations¶
docs.text: Map effect to the sign annotation and put the imported interactions in a slice named prior. Confidence and evidence remain ordinary edge attributes. There is no weight mapping here, so structural weights remain 1.

docs.title: Attribute reads and writes¶
docs.text:
anet.attrs.row returns a detached dictionary; tables are detached too. A change to a returned object does not update the graph. Write with update to merge fields, replace to replace the table of an address, or delete to remove attributes and keep the graph elements. annnet validates a batch before it changes the graph.

The examples select Polars. pandas and PyArrow are also supported. Table operations such as .select() are specific to the selected library.

docs.title: Select evidence and inspect a graph view¶
docs.text: Keep confidence at least 0.85. This threshold is an illustrative analysis choice. The selection retains the condition; the view exposes the corresponding graph, including the endpoints of its selected edges.

docs.title: Compose predicates and choose a boundary¶
docs.text:
Selections support & (intersection), | (union), and - (difference), and retain their graph and axis. Operators include equality, membership, ordered comparisons, and isnull. A missing value only satisfies isnull=True.

For a node selection, a closed view retains only edges wholly inside it. An open view includes touching edges and their full endpoints for one hop. Hyperedges are kept whole or excluded. A nested view can only narrow its parent.

docs.title: Observe what stays live¶
docs.text: Materialize the current view before changing the evidence score of EGFR–AKT. The parent edit makes that record pass the threshold. The live view gains it; the independent graph retains the earlier selection.

docs.title: Save the selected graph¶
docs.text: The example writes into a temporary directory, so you can run it again. To keep an analysis, use your own path. The native format keeps IDs and annotations, so the reopened graph has the selected edges and the label of ERK.

docs.title: Computation and storage¶
docs.text:
Which nodes lie on shortest paths through the imported network? Project the prior to NetworkX, compute betweenness, attach the result by node ID, and save both a native graph and an exchange file for Cytoscape.

Requires annnet[polars,storage,networkx] and the guide data in a data/ directory beside this notebook. The result describes this teaching topology, not a biological ranking.

docs.title: What an export represents¶
docs.text:
A backend graph is a projection of one annnet context. Binary graph libraries cannot directly express every hyperedge, node-layer value, or named slice. Choose the algorithm input before you interpret its output:

Hyperedge mode Representation and consequence skip Omits the relation from computation. reify / star Adds a relation node; paths and node statistics include it. expand / clique Adds pairwise connections; the pairs alone lose the original grouping.

Adapters have defaults: the NetworkX and igraph adapters use skip. With explicit participant coefficients, expansion fails unless you accept the loss with coefficients='drop'. Also decide whether to keep parallel edges, how to aggregate them if not, and how to represent mixed direction or layers. An export can support reconstruction and still be the wrong input for an algorithm.

docs.title: Make the algorithm input explicit¶
docs.text: Select the prior slice and state the hyperedge policy. This dataset contains only binary edges, so skip removes none. If you later introduce hyperedges, reconsider the projection. Keep the returned manifest for re-import.

docs.title: Use a cached accessor when convenient¶
docs.text: anet.nx combines projection and dispatch. For this call, explicitly select the same slice. Clear the accessor after edits before requesting a new projection: current automatic invalidation does not cover every removal or attribute change. Fresh an.to_nx calls avoid that cache.

docs.title: Save the annotated analysis and export for Cytoscape¶
docs.text:
The native object is the analysis artifact. CX2/) is an exchange format for Cytoscape; reify makes hyperedges explicit as relation nodes for that consumer. annnet writes the reconstruction metadata into the CX2 output.

The example writes into a temporary directory, so you can run it again. To keep the files, use your own analysis directory.

docs.title: Persistence and reconstruction channels¶
docs.text:
Use the native .annnet format to resume work in annnet. JSON/NDJSON, Parquet, and CX2 also keep reconstruction extensions inside their output. Runtime graph adapters return a separate manifest; GraphML, GEXF, SIF, CSV, and Excel can write a sidecar file. Keep that metadata with the export. Sidecars contain a checksum, and annnet refuses a sidecar that does not match the main file.

SBML and PyTorch Geometric serve domain-specific tasks and have different limits. The format comparison in the API reference shows what each route can keep.

The native writer materializes attached measurement arrays only for existing node-layer placements. Use attached='error' to refuse that operation, or attached='drop' to leave out the backings. Save an external assay separately when it contains values outside those placements. The writer can reconstruct matrices from structure records; matrix=True also saves the matrix, which makes loading faster and the file larger.

docs.title: History, snapshots, and reproducibility¶
docs.text:
History records some mutating calls, not every edit. Current hooks can miss removals, attribute updates, and slice creation. Snapshots compare sets of node, edge, and slice IDs. They do not capture a full revision or support replay.

The next example demonstrates the distinction: an attribute-only edit changes the graph while leaving a membership diff empty; removing an edge changes that diff. Retain the input files, analysis code, parameters, package versions, and saved graph alongside any history export.

docs.title: Graph model and matrices¶
docs.text:
Import a network, learn what its identities and relationships mean, and read its numerical representations. This notebook covers binary edges, direction, parallel evidence, hyperedges, coefficients, and the matrix mappings used in computation. Small constructed examples make the less common shapes visible.

Requires annnet[polars]. The guide data are synthetic teaching data: put the CSV files in a data/ directory beside this notebook. Start with the quickstart if this is your first use of annnet.

docs.title: Identities and relationships¶
docs.text:
In the tutorial data, egfr_grb2 and egfr_grb2_alt both connect EGFR to GRB2. They remain separate edges because they have different IDs. This is useful when two evidence records or mechanisms share endpoints: an analysis can select or annotate each one independently.

Supply the source's edge-ID column when it provides suitable identifiers. Without one, from_edge_frame derives IDs from each row's content, including the imported annotations and context. Reordering identical rows preserves their derived IDs; changing a recorded value can change the ID. Row-derived IDs are therefore unsuitable as permanent identifiers for records whose contents change.

anet.N addresses ordinary nodes and anet.E addresses structural edges. anet.E.at(edge_id) returns an edge record containing its endpoints, kind, direction, and weight. In a flat graph an endpoint is a node ID. In a layered graph it is a placement, (node_id, layer_coordinate).

Relationship Meaning Directed binary edge One source connected to one target. Undirected binary edge A connection with no direction. Parallel edges Distinct edge IDs connecting the same endpoints. Self-loop The same entity is the source and target. Undirected hyperedge One relationship involving a set of members. Directed hyperedge One relationship connecting a source group to a target group.

Direction can be specified per edge. The graph's directed setting supplies a default, so one container can mix directed and undirected relationships.

docs.title: When a pair of endpoints is insufficient¶
docs.text: A complex or a reaction may involve several participants in one relation. Representing it as independent pairs loses the fact that those participants belong together. A hyperedge retains that grouping:

docs.title: Structure and numerical representations¶
docs.text:
annnet stores each edge's participants, their roles, and coefficients. Sparse matrices are built from that structure when requested. Several matrices serve different purposes:

Property Rows × columns Contents anet.B Entities × binary/node-edge relations Signed coefficient incidence for those edge kinds. anet.H Entities × hyperedges Unsigned membership, one contribution per participant role. anet.S Entities × all structural edges Stored incidence coefficients, including hyperedges. anet.A Entities × entities Weighted adjacency; hyperedges and one-sided edges are excluded by default. anet.L Entities × entities D - A, where D contains row sums of anet.A.

For an ordinary directed edge of weight w, incidence contributes +w at the source and -w at the target. An undirected edge contributes +w on both sides. Explicit participant coefficients can override these values. The stored coefficient sign alone is therefore insufficient to infer endpoint roles.

A directed self-loop has two roles on the same entity. Its two incidence contributions cancel, while its adjacency entry remains on the diagonal. A zero column or a column summing to zero is not a reliable self-loop test; read the endpoints. Ordinary directed edges also have column sum zero.

Weights are already present in coefficient incidence. Do not multiply by a second weight matrix and assume the result equals anet.A or anet.L. In particular, anet.L uses the adjacency definition above, not the product of the unsigned incidence matrix with its transpose.

Use anet.matrices.signed() or another named matrix method when you need the identity-to-position mappings alongside the matrix. Positions describe that materialization and can change after edits. Keep IDs in annotations and saved results.

docs.title: Participant coefficients¶
docs.text: A reaction-style model often uses negative coefficients for consumed species and positive coefficients for produced species. This differs from the default incidence sign convention above. Set coefficients explicitly and continue to read roles from the edge record. The coefficient matrix is derived state; use set_edge_coeffs rather than modifying a returned sparse matrix.

docs.title: Self-loops retain structure even when incidence cancels¶
docs.text: Add a directed self-loop and use the matrix's own identity maps to inspect it. The loop has a zero coefficient column and a nonzero adjacency entry.

docs.title: An edge as an endpoint¶
docs.text: A placeholder edge entity allows another relation to refer to a named object before its participants are defined. It occupies entity space but contributes no structural incidence column of its own.

docs.title: Inspect local connectivity¶
docs.text: On the imported binary network, traversal helpers answer questions without a backend conversion. These queries concern connectivity; an inhibitory sign does not reverse the direction.

docs.title: Layers: coordinates, coupling, measurements, and mathematics¶
docs.text:
A node can occur in several conditions, timepoints, or compartments. A multilayer graph makes those placements explicit and can connect them. This chapter develops the coordinate model, imports a two-layer network, attaches measurements, selects regions, and computes with its supra-matrices.

Requires annnet[polars,storage] and the guide data in a data/ directory beside this notebook. The notebook does not depend on the other guide chapters. The examples use simplified signaling data and do not show biological relations between experimental conditions.

docs.title: The coordinate model¶
docs.text:
Let $V$ be the set of node identities and $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ the labels of the aspects. The possible layer coordinates form $L=L_1\times\cdots\times L_d$. The placements actually present are a subset $V_M\subseteq V\times L$. Declaring the labels does not create the whole product.

For condition, ERK in ('control',) and ERK in ('treated',) are different placements of one node. With time and condition, a coordinate could be ('6h', 'treated'). Tuple order follows the aspect declarations; anet.at lets you address existing placements by aspect name instead.

Edge endpoints Role Same layer Intra-layer Different nodes in different layers Inter-layer Same node in different layers Coupling

A present, isolated placement is different from an absent one. Use anet.layers.place to register isolated placements. Generic node attributes apply to the identity across placements; node_layers attributes belong to one pair.

Slices name sets of existing elements. They suit multiple analysis results over one network. Layers change endpoint identity, and are useful when a method needs separate placements or inter-layer connections.

docs.title: Prepare contextual edge batches¶
docs.text: Declare the condition labels, then convert table endpoints to explicit (node_id, layer_coordinate) pairs. We reuse the same prior in both conditions for this example. With condition-specific input, select the corresponding rows instead. The ID suffix distinguishes each placed interaction.

docs.title: Attach a labeled measurement array¶
docs.text: The CSV has nodes in rows and conditions in columns. attach_values expects layers in rows and nodes in columns, so transpose the numerical block and pass both sets of labels. The array is borrowed rather than copied.

docs.title: Add coupling only when the model needs it¶
docs.text: For illustration, connect each node to its counterpart in the other condition with weight 0.2. This could express an analysis assumption about continuity; it is not inferred from the measurements and is not evidence of causality. Keep these introduced edges in a separate slice.

docs.title: Edge kinds¶
docs.text:
annnet sets the multilayer kind of each edge from its two endpoints. You do not give it:

endpoints kind different nodes in the same layer intra the same node in different layers coupling different nodes in different layers inter

The ml_kind column of the edge table shows the kind. The prior network gives the intra edges, the coupling step the coupling edges. An edge from ('ERK', ('control',)) to ('DUSP6', ('treated',)) would be inter.

docs.title: Choose a boundary¶
docs.text: The closed treatment view contains its 11 intra-layer edges and excludes coupling to control. An open boundary also includes touching coupling edges and their full endpoints. It therefore reaches beyond the treatment layer.

docs.title: Supra-adjacency and its blocks¶
docs.text:
A supra-matrix puts the placements on ordinary matrix axes. For binary edges, $A_{ij}$ is the sum of weights from placement $i$ to $j$. Undirected edges contribute in both directions. Parallel edges add; their individual identities remain available in the graph even when the matrix combines their weights.

With coordinates grouped by condition, our graph has the block form

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}A_{control}&\omega I\\\omega I&A_{treated}\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \omega=0.2.$$

The cross-layer identity blocks arise because each coupling joins the same node across conditions. Other inter-layer relationships would have a different pattern. This example contains no hyperedges; projecting hyperedges to a pairwise operator requires its own policy.

docs.title: Laplacian and a random walk¶
docs.text:
For this nonnegative adjacency, set $D_{ii}=\sum_j A_{ij}$. The combinatorial Laplacian is $L=D-A$. Its rows sum to zero. kind='norm' provides $I-D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}$; symmetric spectral interpretations require an appropriate undirected model, which our directed prior is not.

The transition matrix is $P=D^{-1}A$ on rows with positive degree. Here every placement has a coupling neighbor, so all rows sum to one. For a graph with an isolated placement, the API leaves its row zero; choose a dangling-node policy before claiming that probability is conserved. Negative weights likewise need a different interpretation.

docs.title: Several aspects and an ordered window¶
docs.text: An aspect is categorical by default. Declare an order for time or dose when queries should compare positions. The order is ordinal, not a declaration of elapsed time. The following small table has two timepoints in treatment; the control labels exist but no control placements are created.

docs.title: Save the placed measurements¶
docs.text:
The native writer materializes attached values for existing placements. All pairs in this small matrix have placements, so the layer coordinates and the measurements stay after the round trip. A larger external assay can include pairs without placements; keep that assay separately.

The example writes into a temporary directory. To keep the file, use your own path.

New edges go into an explicit slice= or the active slice. The edge itself is global structure. With propagate=, other slices also get it: 'shared' adds it to each slice that holds both endpoints, 'all' to each slice that holds one or both of them. A global remove_edges call would remove an edge from every slice. To revise one result, update that slice's membership or contextual annotations.

Use slices when several analyses refer to the same interaction identities. Continue with Layers when endpoint placements and connections between coordinates are part of the model.

docs.title: Slices and analysis contexts¶
docs.text:
Which interactions differ between two analysis results, and how do their activities compare? Import one network and join a result table onto its edge IDs. Each condition gets a slice and its own edge annotations.

The notebook uses the same synthetic guide data as Annotations, selections, and views: put the CSV files in a data/ directory beside this notebook. The activities are invented values. The notebook requires annnet[polars] and does not depend on the other guide chapters.

docs.title: What a slice represents¶
docs.text:
A slice is a named membership set over the graph's existing identities. Several slices can include one edge without duplicating its topology. This makes slices useful for prior networks, selected solutions, train/test partitions, and alternative annotations or weighting schemes.

A layer, in contrast, is a coordinate of an endpoint placement. Use a slice when an analysis selects existing interactions; use layers when separate placements and connections between them belong to the model. The two can be combined.

Creating a slice from selection IDs records membership at that moment. It does not retain the selection's predicate. Later confidence updates do not rewrite the slice automatically.

docs.title: Read the result table¶
docs.text: Each row names an existing edge, a condition, and an activity. A missing row means the analysis did not select that edge in that condition. Activity zero would be a measured value, not an instruction to omit the edge.

docs.title: Store membership and values separately¶
docs.text: The loop handles one condition per batch. Slice membership records which edges were selected. edge_slices stores each activity under (condition, edge_id). The original confidence, sign, and structural weight remain on the base edge.

docs.title: Work on one condition¶
docs.text: A slice view restricts membership and reads current parent annotations. A materialized graph is independent. Here it contains the eight selected treatment edges while the original graph continues to hold the whole prior.

docs.title: Join values or filter membership¶
docs.text: slice= joins contextual attributes onto the edge table; in_slice= filters which edges get rows. An analysis that needs only treatment edges should use the latter. Adding the contextual columns alone does not select a subgraph.

docs.title: Contextual weights and mutation scope¶
docs.text: An edge-slice weight overrides the effective weight in that slice. It does not rewrite the base weight or automatically replace every global matrix. Choose a context-aware operation when those overrides must affect computation.

docs.title: Guide data
docs.text:
These three small CSV files are shared by the quickstart and the Guide notebooks. Download them together to run a notebook outside this repository.

File Contents interactions.csv 11 directed interactions among 10 nodes, including two separately identified EGFR–GRB2 edges. edge_results.csv Illustrative edge activities for two conditions: eight selected edges per condition. node_measurements.csv One value per node in each of the two conditions.

docs.title: Provenance and meaning
docs.text:
This is a synthetic teaching dataset, assembled for the annnet documentation from the signaling examples previously built inside its notebooks. The names evoke a signaling network, but the topology is simplified and the confidence, activity, and measurement values are invented. No biological conclusion should be drawn from them. The files are distributed under the repository's BSD-3-Clause license.

In interactions.csv, effect uses +1 for activation and −1 for inhibition. confidence is an illustrative evidence score; evidence identifies a teaching source. Neither becomes a structural edge weight in these notebooks. Explicit edge_id values keep the two EGFR–GRB2 records distinct and let results refer back to the same interactions.

A missing row in edge_results.csv means the interaction was not selected for that condition. It is different from a selected interaction with activity zero. The node measurements are a separate table: importing edges does not attach these values automatically.

To use your own network, replace the input files and specify your source, target, identifier, and annotation columns at import. Start with the quickstart or Annotations, selections, and views.

This section gives the exact signatures and options of the public functions and classes of annnet. To learn the concepts, start with the Guide.

docs.text:
Import annnet as:

import annnet as an

All names below are in the top-level annnet namespace, unless the name shows a subpackage. A name that is not on this page or on the page of its object is internal: for example a name that begins with an underscore, or a module such as annnet.core._store. Internal names can change without notice.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
annnet raises the standard Python exceptions, with a message that names the problem:

situation exception An unknown node, edge, slice, aspect, layer or attribute key. KeyError A key or argument of the wrong shape or type. A predicate that compares values that cannot be compared. A node selection given where edges are expected. TypeError A reserved field. A key that occurs two times in one batch. A missing or null key column. delete without keys and without names. An ordering operator on a categorical aspect. A selection from another graph. A bad boundary, limit, layout or operator. ValueError A write through a view. ReadOnlyViewError, a subclass of TypeError A name that annnet removed. AttributeError, with the name to use instead

docs.title: graph-tool adapter
docs.text: Convert between an AnnNet object and a graph-tool graph. graph-tool holds nodes and binary edges, with one direction for the whole graph and a weight edge property. to_graphtool also gives back a manifest with everything else: hyperedges, the direction of each edge, layers, slices and the attribute tables. Give the manifest to from_graphtool to rebuild the full graph. graph-tool is not on PyPI: install it with conda or your system package manager. To run a graph-tool algorithm without converting yourself, use anet.gt.

docs.title: annnet.adapters.graphtool_adapter.from_graphtool
docs.text:
from_graphtool(
    gtG,
    manifest=None,
    *,
    node_id_property="id",
    edge_id_property="id",
    weight_property="weight"
)

Convert graph_tool.AnnNet (+ optional manifest) back into AnnNet AnnNet.

  • Nodes: from node property node_id_property if present, else numeric index.
  • Edges: from edges in gtG; edge_id from edge property edge_id_property if present, else auto; weight from edge property weight_property if present, else 1.0.

If manifest is provided, rehydrates: - all attribute tables (node/edge/slice/edge_slice/layer), - _slices internal structure, - hyperedges, - edge_directed and edge_direction_policy, - multilayer (aspects, elem_layers, VM, aspect attrs, layer-tuple attrs, edge_kind, edge_layers, node-layer attrs), - graph_attributes.

to_graphtool(

    *,
    node_id_property="id",
    edge_id_property="id",
    weight_property="weight"
)

Convert an AnnNet AnnNet -> (graph_tool.AnnNet, manifest).

graph-tool graph: - nodes: only entities whose kind is a node - edges: only binary edges whose endpoints are such nodes - node property vp[node_id_property] = AnnNet node id - edge property ep[edge_id_property] = AnnNet edge id - edge property ep[weight_property] = edge weight (float)

manifest: - preserves everything graph-tool cannot: hyperedges, slices, multilayer, and ALL attribute tables.

docs.title: annnet.adapters.igraph_adapter.to_igraph
docs.text:
to_igraph(
    graph,
    directed=True,
    hyperedge_mode="skip",
    hyperedges=None,
    coefficients="error",
    slice=None,
    slices=None,
    public_only=False,
    reify_prefix="he::",
)

Export AnnNet → (igraph graph, manifest).

from_igraph takes the manifest as its second argument, so from_igraph(*to_igraph(anet)) is the round trip.

hyperedges : str, optional The same choice as hyperedge_mode, under the name every exporter shares, and accepting "star" and "clique" as aliases for "reify" and "expand". Takes precedence when both are given. coefficients : {"error", "drop"}, default "error" What to do when the projection would drop per-member coefficients. Only "expand" loses them, and losing them silently is what this refuses. hyperedge_mode: {"skip","expand","reify"} - "skip": drop HE edges from igG (manifest keeps them) - "expand": cartesian product (directed) / clique (undirected) - "reify": add a node per HE and membership edges V↔HE carrying roles/coeffs

docs.title: Traversal and structure
docs.text: The traversal methods (neighbors, in_neighbors, out_neighbors, successors, predecessors) are methods of the graph: anet.neighbors('EGFR'). The functions in annnet.algorithms answer questions about the directed edges of a graph.

docs.title: annnet.algorithms.traversal.Traversal
docs.text:
Local neighborhood traversal over the incidence-backed graph.

Every method here delegates to the structural query facade of the core, which owns the traversal itself. The facade answers a binary edge from the adjacency index in time proportional to the degree, and it answers a hyperedge from a list it caches against the structural clock. A graph with no hyperedge therefore never pays a full edge scan.

Yield (source_id, target_id) for every directed binary edge.

An undirected edge has two sides in storage order and no direction, so it is left out. A hyperedge has no single source and no single target, so it is left out too, as are edges incident to edge entities. Ids are bare node ids, whatever layer the node sits in.

directed_cycle(graph)

One directed cycle, as the nodes along it, or None when there is none.

Depth-first over the directed binary edges, stopping at the first cycle found. The list starts and ends on the same node, so a self-loop comes back as [node, node]. Which cycle is found when there are several is not promised.

docs.title: Adding edges
docs.text:
anet.add_edges adds one edge, or a batch of edges. This page lists the input forms and options it accepts. To make a graph from a table of edges, use from_edge_frame. The graph model guide explains edges, hyperedges and the incidence matrix.

A call with one edge returns the edge ID as a string. A batch returns a list of IDs. A node that does not exist yet is created.

docs.title: Binary edge
docs.text:
anet.add_edges('A', 'B')
anet.add_edges('A', 'B', weight=0.5, edge_id='e1', directed=True)

docs.title: Edge between layers
docs.text:
anet.add_edges(('A', ('healthy',)), ('B', ('treated',)))

Each endpoint is a (node_id, layer) pair. On a graph with aspects, always give the pairs. annnet sets the multilayer kind of the edge (see edge kinds in the layers guide):

endpoints kind same node ID, different layers coupling same layer, different node IDs intra different node IDs and layers inter

docs.title: Undirected hyperedge
docs.text: anet.add_edges(['A', 'B', 'C'])

docs.title: Directed hyperedge
docs.text: anet.add_edges(['A', 'B'], ['C', 'D'])  # sources, then targets

docs.title: Edge with coefficients
docs.text:
anet.add_edges({'glucose': -1.0, 'atp': -1.0}, {'glucose-6p': 1.0, 'adp': 1.0})

The first dictionary is the source side, the second the target side. annnet writes the coefficients into the incidence matrix as they are. Only a call with one edge accepts this form.

docs.title: Edge entity without endpoints
docs.text:
anet.add_edges(None, None, as_entity=True, edge_id='virtual_e1', role='enzyme')

This makes an edge that has no endpoints yet. Another edge can use it as an endpoint. edge_id is necessary.

docs.title: A batch of edges
docs.text: Give one list or generator as the only positional argument.

docs.title: Binary edges
docs.text:
# 2-tuples
anet.add_edges([('A', 'B'), ('C', 'D')])

# 3-tuples: the third item is the weight
anet.add_edges([('A', 'B', 0.5), ('C', 'D', 2.0)])

# dictionaries, with the keys source/target or src/tgt
anet.add_edges(
    [
        {'source': 'A', 'target': 'B', 'weight': 0.5, 'edge_id': 'e1'},
        {'src': 'C', 'tgt': 'D'},
    ]
)

docs.title: Hyperedges
docs.text:
A list in src without tgt is an undirected hyperedge. A list in src and a list in tgt is a directed hyperedge. source and target are the same as src and tgt.

anet.add_edges(
    [
        {'src': ['A', 'B', 'C']},  # undirected
        {'src': ['B', 'D'], 'edge_id': 'h2'},  # undirected
        {'src': ['A', 'B'], 'tgt': ['C']},  # directed
    ]
)

A batch can mix binary edges and hyperedges.

docs.title: Edge entities without endpoints
docs.text:
Give dictionaries without source and target, and set as_entity=True. edge_id is optional.

anet.add_edges(
    [
        {'edge_id': 'EE1', 'role': 'enzyme', 'pathway': 'glycolysis'},
        {'edge_id': 'EE2', 'role': 'enzyme', 'pathway': 'tca'},
    ],
    as_entity=True,
    slice='Healthy',
)

In a batch item, the keys other than edge_id, slice, weight, edge_directed, edge_type and propagate are edge attributes.

docs.title: One edge
docs.text: option default description weight 1.0 The edge weight. In the incidence matrix: +weight on the source side and -weight on the target side of a directed edge, +weight on all members of an undirected edge. Not used for an edge with coefficients. edge_id automatic The edge ID. If the ID exists, annnet updates that edge. directed None The direction of this edge. None uses the default of the graph, and then True. parallel 'update' What to do when edge_id is None and the endpoints already have an edge. See below. slice active slice The slice that gets the edge. annnet creates the slice if it does not exist. as_entity False Make the edge an entity that other edges can use as an endpoint. propagate 'none' Which other slices get the edge. See below. flexible None Set the direction from an attribute value. See below. other keywords Edge attributes.

docs.title: Batch
docs.text: option default description default_weight 1.0 The weight of an item that does not give one. default_edge_directed None The direction of an item that does not give one. default_propagate 'none' The propagate value of an item that does not give one. default_slice_weight None The slice weight of an item that does not give one. slice active slice The slice of an item that does not give one. layer None The layer of the items. as_entity False Make all edges entities.

docs.title: parallel
docs.text:
Only for one edge, and only when edge_id is None.

value result 'update' (default) If the endpoints already have an edge, annnet updates that edge and returns its ID. 'parallel' annnet adds a new edge. 'error' If the endpoints already have an edge, annnet raises ValueError.

With an edge_id that exists, annnet updates that edge. With a new edge_id, annnet adds a new edge. If parallel='error' and the endpoints already have a different edge, annnet raises ValueError.

docs.title: propagate
docs.text:
value result 'none' (default) Only the slice in slice gets the edge. 'shared' Each slice that holds both endpoints also gets the edge. 'all' Each slice that holds one or both endpoints also gets the edge.

The slices guide shows an example.

docs.title: flexible
docs.text:
The value of an edge attribute sets the direction of the edge.

anet.add_edges(
    'A',
    'B',
    score=-0.4,
    flexible={
        'var': 'score',  # the attribute to read
        'threshold': 0.0,  # compare the value to this number
        'scope': 'edge',  # read it from the edge
        'above': 's->t',  # direction when the value is above the threshold
        'tie': 'undirected',  # when the value is equal to the threshold
    },
)

above is 's->t' (from source to target) or 't->s'. Below the threshold, the direction is the opposite. tie is 'keep', 'undirected', 's->t' or 't->s'. With 'scope': 'node', annnet compares the attribute of the source node to that of the target node.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: limit detail Coefficients in a batch Only a call with one edge takes the form with coefficients. A batch raises TypeError. parallel in a batch A batch adds each item as a new edge, also when the endpoints already have an edge. A batch does not accept parallel=, and raises TypeError. flexible in a batch A batch does not accept flexible=, and raises TypeError. Items without endpoints In a batch, they need as_entity=True, else annnet raises ValueError. One edge without endpoints It needs edge_id, else annnet raises ValueError. In a batch, annnet makes the ID.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
anet.attrs holds all attributes of a graph, at eight addresses: nodes, edges, slices, aspects, layers, edge_slices, node_layers and elementary_layers. You read and write each address the same way:

  • a read (nodes, table, row, rows) gives a copy;
  • a write is a named call (update, replace, delete);
  • select is a live query, and from_frame makes a fixed selection from the rows of a table that you filtered yourself.

anet.attrs is an Attrs object. select and from_frame give a RowSelection, and schema gives a Schema. The annotations guide shows the use.

docs.title: Addresses
docs.text:
An address is the thing that a set of attributes belongs to. Each address has its key:

address key key columns in a table nodes node_id node_id edges edge_id edge_id slices slice_id slice_id aspects aspect aspect layers layer coordinate tuple layer edge_slices (slice_id, edge_id) slice_id, edge_id node_layers (node_id, layer) node_id, layer elementary_layers (aspect, label) aspect, elementary_layer 
# Read: each call gives a copy. A change to the copy does not change the graph.
anet.attrs.nodes  # the table of one address; one property for each address
anet.attrs.table('nodes', derived=False, backend=None, columns=None, limit=None, layout=None)
anet.attrs.row('nodes', key)  # one row, as a dict
anet.attrs.rows('nodes', keys=None)  # {key: dict}
anet.attrs.schema('nodes')  # the keys and fields, without a table

# Write
anet.attrs.update('nodes', {key: {...}, ...})  # merge the given fields
anet.attrs.replace('nodes', table)  # replace all attributes of the address
anet.attrs.delete('nodes', keys=None, names=None)  # remove attributes

# Select
anet.attrs.select('nodes', score__gte=0.5)  # a live selection
anet.attrs.from_frame('nodes', frame)  # a fixed selection

anet.attrs has no item access, and you cannot assign to its table properties. anet.attrs['nodes'] and anet.attrs.nodes = table raise TypeError, with the name of the call to use.

docs.title: Rules for writes
docs.text:
• A null value removes the field. If update gets None or NaN for a field, annnet removes the field from the row. A null cell in a table means the same.

  • delete removes attributes, never elements. The node, edge, slice or layer stays. The return value is the number of rows that lost an attribute.

    keys names result given not given remove all attributes of these rows not given given remove these fields from all rows given given remove these fields from these rows not given not given ValueError

    An empty keys or names selects nothing. A name that the address does not have raises KeyError. - replace needs the key columns of the address. A key that the table does not have loses its attributes. A table never adds or removes elements. - A write is all or nothing. annnet checks the full write before it changes anything. If one part fails, the attributes, the fields and their types, and the cached matrices stay as they were. - Reserved fields are refused with ValueError: the key columns, and for edges source, target, head, tail, members, weight, directed, kind, slice, slice_weight, flexible and edge_type. - Keys are checked. An unknown key raises KeyError, a key of the wrong shape TypeError, and a key that occurs two times in one write ValueError. For node_layers, give (node_id, layer), or a node ID with layer= in update.

docs.title: Derived tables
docs.text:
table(address, derived=True) adds what the graph knows about each row. For edges, these columns: kind (binary, hyper or node_edge), directed, weight, ml_kind (intra, inter or coupling), source, target, src_layer, dst_layer, head, tail and members.

With layout='incidences', the table has one row for each endpoint of each edge: edge_id, position, entity_id, entity_kind, layer, layer_id, role, coefficient, kind and directed. You can join an endpoint to its node, layer and edge rows without parsing.

limit= builds that number of rows and no more: use it for a preview, not as a selection. The arguments slice=, in_slice=, layer=, include_hyper=, include_binary=, include_directed=, include_weight= and resolved_weight= apply to the derived edge table only.

docs.title: A live query and a filtered table
docs.text:
select is a query on the graph. It keeps its conditions, and gives a new result after the graph changes. A table from anet.attrs.table is a copy of one moment. To filter it, use your dataframe library, then make a selection from the result:

table = anet.attrs.table('nodes')
kept = table.filter(pl.col('score') > 0.5)
chosen = anet.attrs.from_frame('nodes', kept)  # a fixed selection

from_frame reads only the key columns. It gives the keys of the frame, in the order of the address, without repeats. It does not keep the filter: a node that you add later is not in it. A missing key column or a null key raises ValueError, an unknown key KeyError.

A selection of node_layers or edge_slices changes into a selection of another address only with project: select('node_layers', ...).project('nodes'), select('edge_slices', ...).project('edges') or .project('slices').

docs.title: Predicates
docs.text:
All select calls (anet.N.select, anet.E.select, anet.attrs.select, anet.layers.where) take the same conditions: field=value, or field__operator=value. The operators are eq, ne, in, not_in, lt, lte, gt, gte and isnull.

  • A null value matches only isnull=True.
  • An ordered aspect compares labels in their declared order. An ordering operator on a categorical aspect raises ValueError.
  • An unknown field raises KeyError. Values that cannot be compared raise TypeError.
  • For a field name that contains __, give a mapping with (field, operator) keys.

docs.title: annnet.core._predicate
docs.text:
The one predicate engine every selection surface shares.

anet.N.select(score__gt=0.5), anet.E.select(kind='hyper'), anet.attrs.select('node_layers', score__gte=0.8) and anet.layers.where(time__lte='12h') are four spellings of one question: which rows of this axis satisfy these conditions. They parse the conditions here, evaluate them here, and report a bad field, operator or value the same way.

A condition is field=value (equality) or field__operator=value with one of :data:OPERATORS. A literal field whose own name contains __ wins over suffix parsing, and a positional mapping may use explicit (field, operator) keys where a keyword would be ambiguous.

Null handling is one rule everywhere: a missing value — None or a float NaN — is excluded by every comparison, including ne and not_in, and selected only by an explicit field__isnull=True.

An ordered aspect compares by its declared order, through order=; a categorical aspect refuses the four ordering operators. A numeric attribute compares numerically. Two values that cannot be compared raise, naming the field and the operator, rather than silently dropping the row.

    "ne",
    "in",
    "not_in",
    "lt",

    "gt",

docs.title: Backend accessors
docs.text:
An AnnNet object gives access to the algorithms of three graph libraries:

accessor library what anet.<accessor>.<name> calls anet.nx NetworkX the function networkx.<name>, for example from the NetworkX algorithms anet.ig igraph the method igraph.Graph.<name> of the converted graph (see the Graph API and graph analysis), or else the function igraph.<name> anet.gt graph-tool the function graph_tool.<namespace>.<name>, called as anet.gt.<namespace>.<name>

The accessor converts anet to a graph of the library, calls the function, and gives back the result of the library. The conversion is cached.

# networkx.betweenness_centrality(...)
scores = anet.nx.betweenness_centrality(anet)

# igraph.Graph.pagerank() on the converted graph
pagerank = anet.ig.pagerank()

# graph_tool.centrality.pagerank(...)
pagerank = anet.gt.centrality.pagerank(anet)

Pass anet where the library function expects its graph. The accessor puts the converted graph in its place. Where the library takes a node, you can give the annnet node ID.

The graph-tool namespaces are those of the graph-tool documentation: topology, centrality, clustering, flow, inference, generation, search and util. A name that only one namespace has also works without the namespace: anet.gt.pagerank(anet).

docs.title: Accessors and adapters
docs.text:
The adapter functions in annnet.adapters also convert, but they give you the graph of the other library:

  • annnet.adapters.to_nx(...) and annnet.adapters.from_nx(...)
  • annnet.adapters.to_igraph(...) and annnet.adapters.from_igraph(...)
  • annnet.adapters.to_graphtool(...) and annnet.adapters.from_graphtool(...)

Use an adapter when you want to work with the other graph object yourself. Use anet.nx, anet.ig or anet.gt when anet stays your data and you only want the result of an algorithm.

Clear the cache after a change

Not every change of anet clears the cached conversion. After you edit the graph, call clear() on the accessor before you run another algorithm, or convert again with an adapter. The computation guide shows both forms.

docs.title: Methods of every accessor
docs.text:
• backend(...): the converted graph of the library.
  • clear(): remove the cached conversions of this accessor.

anet.nx and anet.ig also have:

  • peek_nodes(k=10): a few node identifiers of the converted graph.

docs.title: Conversion options
docs.text:
anet.nx.backend(...) and anet.ig.backend(...) take these options:

  • directed
  • hyperedge_mode
  • slice
  • slices
  • needed_attrs
  • simple
  • edge_aggs

An algorithm call takes the same options with a prefix, so that they do not mix with the arguments of the library function: _nx_directed, _nx_hyperedge, _nx_slice, _nx_slices, _nx_label_field, _nx_simple and _nx_edge_aggs for NetworkX, and the same names with _ig_ for igraph.

# Betweenness on the graph read as undirected
scores = anet.nx.betweenness_centrality(anet, _nx_directed=False)

anet.gt.backend() takes no options and gives the converted graph-tool graph.

docs.text:
merge(other)

Take every element of other that this graph does not hold.

This is the in-place union, and it is what anet |= H runs. The graph on the left is the answer wherever the two disagree: an element both graphs hold keeps the attributes it has here, and only an element this graph does not hold arrives with the attributes of other.

Parameters:

The graph to take from. It is not changed.

required

This graph.

docs.text:

Where the two disagree about one element, this graph is the answer. See :meth:merge, which is the same operation without the copy.

docs.title: intersection
docs.text:

Return a graph holding the elements that both graphs hold.

An edge survives only when every node it names does, so an edge both graphs hold is dropped when one of its endpoints is not shared.

docs.title: difference
docs.text:
difference(other)

Return a graph holding the elements other does not hold.

An edge survives only when every node it names does, so an edge that keeps its own id loses its place when an endpoint goes.
